How can understanding Linux improve your chances of landing a decent career in the tech industry?

This is probably the best thing you can do in your free time since you spend every day on a computer anyways.

And I know what you're thinking: where the hell do I even start? There are all kinds of distros and repositories, and where would a total beginner even start?

Start with vmware player. It's software can run on your windows machine, and emulate all sorts of operating systems. Then start googling. Look up "linux tutorial install" and follow one. If you make a mistake or something just didn't work right, who cares, you're doing it in a virtual machine so you can just start over or try something else. You won't learn anything if you don't make mistakes.

Also, linux is the terminal, learn to love it. If you think you can do something in the terminal then do it. It's also a lot more straight forward than trying to wrap your head around different desktop environments and windows managers. You'll learn about all these by downloading different distributions and installing them, and eventually something will click. But the basic commands will all be consistent at a terminal.

Forget certification. All it will do is prepare you for certification exam. If you want to be a front end designer, just create few front end designs and showcase them on a website of your own. That way you will learn the technology hands on and will have a solid resume. If you are aiming to do backend coding you could code a website and show that to your future employer.

Seconded, I learned most of what I know on the job and showing the ability to adapt and problems solve (google and apply) solutions. I've been using Free Code Camp to learn full stack JavaScript development. Codecademy is a good option too, especially if you have previous experience with coding, but you'll have to be more proactive about putting together your portfolio to show to potential employers.

Here's my approach, it can be a bit of a gamble and I personally did not take this path in tech but I know of people who have attracted the attention of Silicon Valley companies using it. It is way more likely to work if you are looking for a startup-software-engineer-type job. This path is more likely to be successful if you are currently in school (as you are).

  1. Think about something cool you would like to build. A personal website, or maybe an app. Have you always been frustrated with the lack of good to-do list apps? Make a better one. The point is, think of it like a weekend project except it'll take way longer than a weekend. Think of it like building a porch, or something.

  2. Figure out what skills you need to build your porch. I'm an on-the-go-learner so I will learn and realize my incompetencies as I come across each new obstacle. Follow tutorials. Learn what you need to build what you envision. Realize you'll need to know about "xml" types? Learn that and apply it. Realize you need to learn to use a jigsaw? Learn that and apply it.

  3. With enough work and time, you will come out with a shitty porch. Don't worry - this is your first porch. The magic of technology means you don't have to burn this porch down - instead, you can actually just build off of it, edit, and improve it. Improve your porch. Figure out what the best porch builders do and do that. Steal ideas and adapt them to your needs.

  4. You've now built an excellent porch and in doing so, learned a lot about building things in general. You've learned woodworking, you've learned to paint, you've learned how to apply a lacquer, you've learned structural design - and now you have marketable skills as well as a product to show off. By porch I mean application, or something... we're still talking about tech, right?

Anyway, try that. Anybody worth working for will respect the working knowledge and tenacity you've gained, even if they don't respect your product. You'll be better equipped than a CS graduate who never built anything outside of class. Tech recruiters and CEOs seem to support this approach but again, it's a gamble. You might just end up wasting a bunch of time and building a damn useless porch.
